strengths: Clear and well-motivated idea: constraining both the key vector (entity-specific subspace via SVD over many subjects) and the residual vector (a low-dimensional subspace governing the object logit) is a natural extension of the locate-then-edit framework grounded in the Linear Representation Hypothesis.

Strong empirical results across three models (LLaMA-3-8B, GPT-J-6B, Qwen2.5-7B) and two benchmarks, with large reported specificity gains over strong recent baselines, especially AlphaEdit (e.g., +43.2 points on LLaMA-3 CounterFact).

Evaluation is more demanding than much prior work: a generation-based (argmax) success criterion, filtering to instances where the model actually knows the fact, and sequential editing over 1000 and 5000 edits with general-capability tracking.

Comprehensive analysis section: token-level perturbation visualizations, quantitative MLP-output perturbation comparison, variance analysis validating the entity-specific/entity-agnostic subspace split, decomposition analysis of the residual vector, hyperparameter tradeoff curves, and ablations of the two components (Table 5).
Extended baseline comparisons (ROME, RECT, PRUNE, NSE, FT-W) and probability-based criterion results in the appendix, plus evaluation on the CHED contextual dataset.
Clear writing and a complete appendix covering the AlphaEdit machinery, regularization details, and derivations of the additive update.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the method is essentially AlphaEdit/MEMIT with modified inputs (projected key vector and low-rank residual vector); the update itself reuses AlphaEdit's closed-form solution. The core contribution is a refinement rather than a new paradigm.

Several design choices feel ad hoc and are weakly justified: why exactly a two-dimensional subspace (w1, w2) for the residual vector is optimal is asserted rather than derived; the additive magnitude-swap update assumes w1 and w2 are orthogonal, but the objective only penalizes their inner product with weight λ, so the Appendix C derivation is approximate in practice.

The per-edit gradient-based optimization to find {w1, w2} undermines the closed-form efficiency appeal of locate-then-edit methods; no runtime/compute cost comparison against MEMIT/AlphaEdit is reported, which is a notable omission for a method that adds a per-edit optimization step.

Evaluation protocol deviates from standard practice (filtering to instances where the pre-edit argmax is o, using a stricter generation-based criterion), making direct comparison with numbers reported in prior papers impossible; all baselines were re-run by the authors, which is good but means the very large gains cannot be cross-checked against the literature.

Some evidence for the subspace hypothesis is thin: the variance-ratio analysis (Table 2) and the component decomposition (Table 4) are suggestive but not conclusive; the finding that w1 and w2 are not actually disentangled (Section 6.2.2) partially undercuts the stated mechanism.

Inconsistencies and noise in reporting: Table 10's harmonic-mean score S=38.0 does not match the reported Eff./Gen./Spe. values; several Qwen/Llama general-capability results in Table 8 show non-trivial degradation for SUIT relative to AlphaEdit on some benchmarks (e.g., SST, MMLU for Qwen) despite claims of robust preservation; no statistical significance, seeds, or variance across runs are reported.

Hyperparameters (τ_energy=0.4, λ=0.3) appear tuned on the evaluation setting, and the sensitivity analysis is only on LLaMA/CounterFact; robustness of these choices across models and datasets is not demonstrated.

Code is only promised upon publication; reproducibility currently depends on the authors' description of the optimization procedure, which has underspecified details (initialization, steps, learning rate for finding w1, w2).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated idea: constraining knowledge edits to entity-specific subspaces and a critical 2D object-encoding subspace, grounded in the Linear Representation Hypothesis, is a sensible and novel refinement of the locate-then-edit paradigm built on AlphaEdit.

Strong empirical results on the main benchmark: on CounterFact, SUIT substantially improves the harmonic mean score over AlphaEdit across three models (e.g., +31 points on LLaMA-3-8B), driven largely by large specificity gains (+43.2 points) while maintaining near-ceiling efficacy.

The evaluation is more rigorous than much prior work: the authors adopt a stricter generation-based (argmax) criterion as the primary metric, report probability-based results in the appendix, evaluate general capability on six benchmarks, include a 5,000-edit sequential setting, and test contextual robustness on CHED.

The analysis section is a genuine strength: variance analysis of subspace components, measurement of the proportion of updates affecting entity-agnostic directions, steering experiments decomposing the residual vector, hyperparameter tradeoff analysis, and component ablations collectively provide good mechanistic validation of the method's assumptions.
Comprehensive baselines (FT, MEND, MEMIT, PMET, AlphaEdit plus extended comparisons with ROME, RECT, PRUNE, NSE) and a promise of code release support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Some methodological choices appear heuristic and under-justified: the restriction of the residual-vector update to exactly a two-dimensional subspace spanned by w1, w2 is a strong assumption; the paper acknowledges w1/w2 are not fully disentangled (each also affects the other object's logit), which somewhat undercuts the clean 'raise new object / suppress old object' narrative.

Results are not uniformly superior: on zsRE, SUIT does not consistently beat AlphaEdit (e.g., lower Generalization on GPT-J and Qwen, lower Specificity on GPT-J/Llama), and GC scores on Qwen degrade notably (30.77 vs. 28.87 pre-edit for some benchmarks is mixed); the headline claims are stronger than the full result pattern.

Potential confound in the comparison: SUIT's key-vector subspace removal is computed from PARAREL subjects and tuned hyperparameters (τenergy, λ) fixed across models; a more careful analysis of sensitivity to the subspace-estimation dataset and of whether AlphaEdit could be given equally tuned tuning is not provided.

The connection between the two mechanisms (key-vector projection and 2D residual update) and the final weight update via Eq. (1) is somewhat loose; it is not fully clear why the closed-form MEMIT/AlphaEdit update with the modified k and δ inherits the desired subspace properties, and the theoretical justification is mostly empirical.

The perturbation analyses (Figures 2-3) are limited to a single model (Llama-3) and small sample sizes/qualitative heatmaps; broader quantitative evidence across models would strengthen the mechanism claims.

Minor writing issues (e.g., 'feaures' in the conclusion, some awkward phrasing, 'Inscrctruct' typo in hyperparameter settings) and the dependence on a regularization term whose hyperparameters' roles overlap between λ and the removed KL/weight-decay terms could confuse readers.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated idea: constraining locate-then-edit updates to edit-relevant subspaces (entity-specific key subspace via SVD-based energy truncation; low-dimensional object-logit-relevant residual subspace) directly targets the known perturbation weakness of MEMIT/AlphaEdit.

Strong and consistent empirical gains: large specificity improvements (e.g., +43.2 points on LLaMA-3-8B COUNTERFACT) while maintaining efficacy, across three models and two benchmarks, with a stricter generation-based (argmax) success criterion.

Thorough supporting analyses: token-level perturbation heatmaps, MLP-output norm comparisons, variance analysis validating entity-specific vs. entity-agnostic subspaces, update-proportion analysis (Table 3), steering analysis for w1/w2, hyperparameter tradeoffs, and a component ablation showing genuine synergy.

Comprehensive evaluation beyond the standard setup: CHED contextual robustness, RippleEdits, a 5,000-edit long-horizon stability study, General Capability benchmarks (MMLU/GLUE), a 13B scaling experiment, and cost analysis of the precomputation.

Careful and transparent treatment of evaluation pitfalls (e.g., detailed discussion of why argmax pre-knowledge checks fail on zsRE, and a stricter token-preservation specificity test in Appendix E.2.2), which increases trust in the reported gains.
weaknesses: The method is largely incremental over MEMIT/AlphaEdit: the update formula is reused from AlphaEdit, and the contributions are modifications of the key and residual vectors rather than a new editing formulation; the theoretical interplay between the modified key k' and AlphaEdit's null-space projection P (precomputed on original keys) is not analyzed and could break the preservation guarantee.

Several design choices are heuristic and weakly justified: why exactly a two-dimensional residual subspace is sufficient, the magnitude-swap additive update, the symmetric assumption h⊤w1 < h⊤w2, and the energy-threshold-based truncation; the paper's own analysis (Section 6.2.2) shows w1/w2 are not actually disentangled, partially undermining the stated hypothesis.

Some headline gains rest on non-standard evaluation choices: the zsRE specificity metric is redefined (using the model's own pre-batch generations as reference), which, while argued for, makes direct comparison with prior reported numbers less meaningful, and no statistical significance/variance across runs is reported.

The k-only vs. δ-only ablation shows δ-only performs poorly (S=68.3), suggesting the two-dimensional residual-vector component is fragile on its own and the key subspace modification carries most of the benefit.

Applicability concerns: precomputation cost (~1.7 hours for N=25.8K subjects on an A100 per model-layer pair) and reliance on PARAReL-derived subject statistics; robustness of the entity-agnostic subspace to domains far from Wikidata is not tested.

strengths: The paper demonstrates substantial empirical gains in specificity over strong baselines (AlphaEdit, MEMIT, PMET) across three models (LLaMA-3-8B, GPT-J-6B, Qwen2.5-7B) on CounterFact, with +43.2 points on LLaMA-3-8B, and further validation on ZSRE, CHED (contextual robustness), and RippleEdits.

The evaluation is broad: sequential editing (1,000 and 5,000 edits), general capability benchmarks (MMLU, GLUE tasks), fluency/consistency metrics, probability-based and generation-based criteria, and a scaling experiment on LLaMA2-13B.

The analysis section makes a genuine effort to validate the core hypotheses empirically: variance analysis of entity-specific vs. entity-agnostic key components, measurement of update leakage into the entity-agnostic subspace (Table 3), steering experiments decomposing δ into parallel/orthogonal components, and ablations showing both components contribute (Table 5).

Practical considerations are addressed: one-time pre-computation cost analysis (Table 15), sensitivity of the subspace to sample size N (Tables 16-17), and hyperparameter trade-off curves with cross-model spectral consistency (Figure 8).
weaknesses: The method's theoretical grounding is thin and heuristic. The claim that the residual update can be confined to a two-dimensional subspace spanned by w1, w2 is an unproven assumption; the paper's own analysis (Section 6.2.2, Figure 7) shows w1 and w2 are not disentangled—w1 also suppresses the old object and w2 promotes the new one—undermining the clean swap-of-magnitudes narrative that motivates the design.

The zsRE specificity evaluation deviates from the established protocol: the authors replace the standard gold-reference metric with a custom 'model's own pre-edit output' reference (Appendix E.2), which makes the headline specificity numbers not directly comparable to prior work. While a stricter test is provided in E.2.2, the modified metric introduces a risk of inflating apparent preservation and weakens comparability with prior literature.

The 43.2-point specificity gain on LLaMA-3-8B CounterFact is striking relative to AlphaEdit, yet the mechanism-level evidence (Table 3) is surprising in that AlphaEdit's updates affect the entity-agnostic subspace more than MEMIT's, despite AlphaEdit's explicit null-space constraint—an apparent tension with AlphaEdit's stated design that is not explained.

Novelty is incremental: the approach is largely a modification of AlphaEdit's update rule via two projection constraints (SVD-based key subspace removal and a 2D residual subspace). Related null-space and perturbation-restrained editing methods (PRUNE, RECT) are closely related, and the paper does not clearly delineate what is fundamentally new beyond the specific projection choices.

Editing instruct models (LLaMA3-Instruct, Qwen2.5-Instruct) with CounterFact yields very low pre-edit general capability scores (e.g., Qwen 28.9, GPT-J 24.3 in Table 1) and unusual baseline behavior (MEND scoring 0.0 almost everywhere), raising questions about the experimental setup and how representative these numbers are.
The energy-threshold hyperparameter τenergy is selected by maximizing the harmonic-mean S on the evaluation data itself (Section 6.3), which risks test-set tuning rather than principled selection.

Some editorial and rigor issues: the entity-agnostic subspace is computed once from Pararel subjects (N=10,000) and assumed universal across relations and datasets; the w1/w2 symmetric constraint argument ('without loss of generality') glosses over ordering issues; and claims like 'setting a new standard for scalable and reliable model editing' overstate what a single-method comparison supports.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated problem (specificity/perturbation in locate-then-edit knowledge editing) and proposes a clean, principled idea grounded in the Linear Representation Hypothesis: decompose the key vector into entity-specific vs. entity-agnostic components and confine the residual update to a low-dimensional critical subspace.

Empirical results are strong and broad: three models (LLaMA-3-8B, GPT-J-6B, Qwen2.5-7B), two benchmarks (CounterFact, zsRE), with a large specificity gain over AlphaEdit (e.g., +43.2 points on LLaMA-3-8B CounterFact) while maintaining high efficacy, fluency, and general capability. Extended results include CHED (contextual robustness), RippleEdits, a 5,000-edit sequential setting, and a LLaMA2-13B scaling experiment, all favorable to SUIT.

The analysis section is unusually thorough and goes beyond headline metrics: variance decomposition validating the entity-specific/entity-agnostic split, a cross-pair entity-vs-context intervention study (Appendix J), steering experiments showing the span(w1,w2) component is more effective per unit norm than the orthogonal component, token-level perturbation visualizations, and per-layer MLP output norm comparisons quantitatively supporting the mechanism claims.

A careful ablation study (Table 5) shows both components (k-only and delta-only) contribute individually and synergistically, and hyperparameter sensitivity analyses (Figure 5, Appendix H) plus a pre-computation cost/sensitivity study (Appendix I, Tables 15-17) support reproducibility and practicality.

The paper is transparent about limitations, e.g., acknowledging that w1 and w2 are not fully disentangled (Section 6.2.2, Appendix G), and the ZSRE-specificity metric issue is analyzed rather than hidden (Appendix E.2).
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the core update mechanism is inherited directly from AlphaEdit (Eq. 1); SUIT's contribution is restricted to modifying the inputs to that formula (subspace-projected key vector and a 2-D constrained residual vector). The contribution is a refinement within an established line (ROME/MEMIT/AlphaEdit) rather than a new editing paradigm, and the similarity of the entity-agnostic subspace idea to AlphaEdit's null-space projection should be more sharply differentiated.

The two-dimensional subspace assumption in Sec. 4.3 (exactly two directions w1, w2, with a magnitude-swap additive update) appears ad hoc; the authors' own analysis (Section 6.2.2, Figure 7) shows the directions are entangled (w1 also suppresses the old object and vice versa), undermining the stated mechanistic hypothesis. No justification or ablation is given for why dimension 2 is optimal versus 1, 3, or k.

The ZSRE specificity evaluation is non-standard: the authors replace the established gold-answer-based metric with one referencing the model's own generated tokens (Appendix E.2), a change made by the authors that could favor their method. Although the stricter preservation test (Table 7) partially mitigates this concern and the gold-reference results are argued to be uninformative, a reviewer must treat headline ZSRE specificity numbers with caution; comparisons to prior published ZSRE numbers are therefore not apples-to-apples.

No statistical rigor: results are single runs with no variance estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests, despite large claimed gaps (e.g., 86.8 vs. 55.8 S-score) and stochastic components (per-edit gradient optimization for delta, subject sampling for the subspace).

Some inconsistencies and loose ends: general capability (GC) scores drop substantially for all methods on Qwen (e.g., SUIT 23.7 vs. pre-edit 20.8 in Table 8 vs. different pre-edit baselines across tables), the LLaMA2-13B comparison reuses LLaMA3-8B hyperparameters for all methods which may disadvantage baselines, and the ablation baselines in Table 5 (k-only/δ-only) are not compared against an analogous AlphaEdit + partial-modification control to isolate the effect of subspace constraints from simply weaker updates.

Reproducibility is currently limited: code and data are only promised 'upon publication,' and the method introduces multiple new hyperparameters (tau_energy, lambda, N=10,000 subjects, directional penalty) whose sensitivity across models is only partially characterized.

Positioning could better discuss closely related subspace/null-space methods (e.g., PRUNE, NSE) which appear only in appendix comparisons; the related-work section is brief on how SUIT's feature-subspace approach differs conceptually from these null-space approaches.
